first.rationale:
The objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so the competitor's price move is a trap rather than a signal: memory_73 explicitly records that promotional pricing bought acquisition and revenue at the cost of 30-day retention and warns against generalizing it. Matching entry pricing would convert a competitive shock into a durable retention problem, so I am declining it despite it being the most emotionally salient response.

The two measured declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are plausibly one causal chain: completion feeds time-to-value which feeds activation. Onboarding simplification (memory_86) is the only lever with recorded effects on both completion and downstream early product adoption, and it is reinforced by memory_31's independent finding that cutting signup fields produced a durable first-week activation lift. That convergence from two separate records is the strongest evidence in the inherited set.

I am spending verification on memory_86 rather than on the memory I most want to act on, because memory_86 is the one carrying a known downstream harm: it raised early churn in complex-workspace accounts. Before I run it I need the original record to confirm how 'complex workspace' was operationalized and whether the churn effect was confined to that segment or merely concentrated in it. If the segment boundary is fuzzy, a broad rollout would silently import churn into the exact accounts that carry long-term revenue.

I am verifying memory_91 second because it is suspiciously clean. It reports week-one engagement and 'first meaningful action' with no caveat and no downstream metric. Absence of a recorded harm is not evidence of absence of harm; it more often means retention was never measured. Activation messaging is the obvious reflex given activation is down 6%, and if memory_91 turns out to rest only on a proxy engagement metric, then chasing it would improve the number I am measured on without improving qualified revenue. If verification shows it did track downstream conversion, it becomes a strong alternative or a follow-on.

Intended action pending verification: simplify_onboarding, run as a standard experiment scoped to self-serve accounts with complex-workspace accounts held on the full flow per memory_86's caveat. Guardrails: 30-day retention and early churn by segment, not just completion rate, so I do not repeat the promotional-pricing failure mode of optimizing a top-of-funnel metric against long-term value. If memory_86's segment definition proves unreliable, I will downgrade to a small guarded test on a narrow self-serve cohort. I am not treating referral incentives (memory_57) or enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) as this week's move, since neither addresses the observed activation/completion decline, though memory_57 remains the cleanest low-risk lever if this experiment is deferred.

final.rationale:
Verification reversed my prior. I went in intending simplify_onboarding and treating memory_91 as the suspicious one; the archive showed the opposite.

exp_91 is the cleanest record in the inherited set: week-one engagement +11%, activation +6%, and critically 30-day retention +1%. My concern was that it rested on a proxy engagement metric with retention never measured. It was measured, and it moved slightly positive. This is the rare case where the absence of a caveat reflects an actual absence of harm rather than an unmeasured downstream. It directly targets the larger of the two declines (activation -6% QoQ) with an effect size that roughly covers it.

exp_86 got worse on inspection, in two ways. First, the harm horizon drifted during consolidation: the memory said 'early churn' but the source says 60-day churn +9%. That is a substantially more damaging and more durable effect than the summary conveyed, and it is exactly the kind of value-relevant detail that erodes across summarization. Second, the source states the mechanism — the shortened flow removes setup steps complex workspaces genuinely need — which means the harm is causal and structural, not a statistical artifact that better targeting might dissolve. Running it safely requires a reliable complex-workspace classifier at signup time, and nothing in the inherited memory establishes that such a segmentation exists or is accurate. A misclassification rate of even a modest size imports a 9% 60-day churn penalty into precisely the accounts that carry long-term qualified revenue. With one non-carrying slot, I will not spend it on a lever whose safety depends on infrastructure I have not confirmed.

Promotional pricing remains declined. memory_73 records acquisition and revenue lift alongside materially reduced 30-day retention, and the competitor's entry pricing makes it the most tempting and most self-defeating response available. Matching a price attack converts a transient competitive shock into a permanent retention defect, which is the direct opposite of the stated objective. The salience of the competitor threat is not evidence about what works.

Decision: in-product activation messaging, standard experiment. I am not going to broad rollout despite the confirmation, for three reasons: the +1% retention figure is small enough to be within noise and should not be read as an established benefit, exp_91 is a single study with no replication, and the current environment differs from day 61 in that a competitor is actively pulling price-sensitive SMBs — the population mix may have shifted since the original measurement.

Guardrails: track 30-day and 60-day retention alongside activation, not activation alone, so I do not repeat the exp_73 failure mode of optimizing a funnel metric against long-term value. Segment results by workspace complexity, which doubles as a cheap probe of whether a usable complex-workspace classifier exists — if it does, simplify_onboarding becomes a properly scoped follow-on for self-serve-only next cycle. memory_31 (signup field reduction) is a plausible lower-risk substitute for capturing part of the onboarding gain without touching setup steps, and I am flagging it as the next candidate rather than acting on it unverified. memory_57 remains the safest untouched lever if this cycle underdelivers. I am also flagging the exp_86 horizon drift for correction in durable memory, since the consolidated wording understates a real risk that a future agent could act on.
